record.question: What is the proposal deadline, and how many copies must be submitted, for the City of Madison (Florida) Police Officers' and Firefighters' Retirement System RFP No. 2025-0901 for investment consulting services?
record.answer:
# Markdown Briefing

## City of Madison (Florida) RFP No. 2025-0901

- **Proposal deadline:** **2:00 p.m. on September 1, 2025**
- **Required submission copies:** **One original and five (5) copies**

## Additional Submission Note

- Proposals received **after 2:00 p.m. on September 1, 2025** will be **returned unopened**.
- The proposal must be submitted in a **sealed envelope or package** addressed to the **City Clerk at the City of Madison**.

RFP No. 2025-0901
Investment Consulting Services
The City of Madison Police Officer’s & Firefighters’ Retirement System (the “Plan”) is a 
governmental defined benefit plan with total assets of $7.07 Million. There are 21 active 
members in the Plan.
The Board of Trustees consist of five (5) members: One police officer, elected by active 
police members of the Plan; one firefighter, elected by active firefighter members of the 
Plan; two City residents, appointed by the City; and one member chosen by the other 
four members. The Board is a governmental entity subject to both the Public Records 
and Sunshine Laws.
Proposals for Investment Consulting Services will be received by the Board of Trustees 
for the City of Madison Police Officer’s & Firefighters’ Retirement System at the office of 
the City Clerk, 321 SW Rutledge Street, Madison, FL 32340 until September 1, 2025.
The Board is soliciting Requests for Proposal (RFP) from investment consulting firms to 
provide general investment advice and counsel regarding the Police Officers’ & 
Firefighters’ Retirement System Trust funds. 
Any proposal received after 2:00 p.m. on September 1, 2025 whether by mail or 
otherwise, will be returned unopened. Proposers are responsible for ensuring that their 
proposal is marked by the Clerk’s office personnel by the deadline indicated.
An original and five (5) copies of the proposal shall be submitted in a sealed 
envelope/package addressed to Lee Anne Hall, City Clerk, City of Madison and clearly 
marked “RFP No. 2025-0901 – Investment Consulting Services”.

Investment Consulting & Management Services
PART I
PROPOSAL TERMS AND CONDITIONS
1-1 Introduction: The Board of Trustees for the City of Madison Police Officer’s & 
Firefighters’ Retirement System (the “Board”) is soliciting Requests for Proposals 
(RFP) for Investment Consulting firms to provide general investment advice, 
counsel and portfolio implementation services to the City of Madison Police Officers’ 
& Firefighters’ Retirement System (the “Plan”). This search was authorized by the 
Board and seeks to identify potential full-service investment consultants. The 
consultants will report to the Board.
1-2 Proposal Submission and Withdrawal: All proposals are subject to the 
conditions specified herein. Those which do not comply with these conditions are 
subject to rejection. The Board must receive all proposals by 2:00 p.m. on 
September 1, 2025. The proposals shall be submitted to the following address: 
City of Madison
City Clerk
321 SE Rutledge Street
Madison, FL 32340
All proposals must be submitted in a sealed envelope. Please clearly mark the 
outside of the proposal package as follows: RFP No. 2025-0901 – Investment 
Consulting Services. The package should also include the proposer’s return 
address.

01259332-1 RFP No. 2025-__ - Investment Consulting and Management Services Page 4
4898-5945-2974, v. 1
Once opened, proposals become property of the City of Madison, Florida (the 
“City”) and the Board and will not be returned to the proposer. 
1-3 Number of Copies: Proposers shall submit an original and five (5) copies.
1-4 Development Costs: Neither the Board, the City of Madison, nor its administrators 
will be responsible nor shall be held liable for any expenses incurred in connection 
with the preparation of responses to this RFP. Proposers should prepare their 
proposals simple and economically, providing a straightforward and concise 
description of the Proposer’s ability to meet the requirements of the RFP. 
1-5 Inquiries: Interested Proposers may contact the Board regarding questions about 
the proposal by email at lanee.pike@cityofmadisonfl.com, Attention: Lanee Pike. 
Written requests for clarification on the meaning or interpretation of the RFP will be 
received until five (5) days prior to the submittal date.
1-6 Addendum: The Board may record its response to inquiries and any supplemental 
instructions in the form of written addenda. The Board may provide written addenda 
up to two (2) days before the date fixed for receiving proposals. Proposers may 
contact the Board to ascertain whether any addenda have been issued. Failure to 
do so may result in an unresponsive proposal. Any oral explanation given before 
the RFP opening will not be binding. 
All proposers are expected to carefully examine the proposal documents. Any 
ambiguities or inconsistencies should be brought to the attention of the Board 
through written communication as soon as possible. 
1-7 Contract Award: The Board anticipates entering into an Agreement with the 
Proposer submitting the proposal judged by the Board to be the most 
advantageous. The Board reserves the right to accept or reject any proposals, with 
or without cause, to waive technicalities or to accept the proposals which, in their 
sole judgment, best serve the interest of the Board, or to award a contract to the 
next most qualified proposer if the successful proposer does not execute a contract 
within sixty (60) days after being notified of the award of the proposal. The Board

4898-5945-2974, v. 1
also reserves the right to abandon the project and/or to solicit and re-advertise for 
other proposals. 
The Proposer understands that this RFP does not constitute an offer or an 
Agreement with the Proposer. An Agreement shall not be deemed to exist and is 
not binding until proposals are reviewed and verified as responsive by appointed 
staff, and the best proposal has been identified, approved by the Board and 
executed by all parties. 
Any proposal may be withdrawn at any time up to five (5) days after the submittal 
date. Any proposal not so withdrawn shall constitute an irrevocable offer for a 
period of six (6) months to provide to the Board the services set forth in the RFP.
1-8 Contractual Agreement: When a proposal is accepted, a contract will be issued 
as proposed, subject to any revisions which may be mutually agreed upon by the 
Board and proposer. This RFP shall be included and incorporated in the final 
award. The order of contractual precedence will be the Contract original Terms and 
Conditions, and proposer response. Venue for any and all legal action to enforce 
the award will be in Madison County, Florida and the contractual obligations will be 
interpreted according to the laws of Florida. Any additional contract or 
agreement requested for consideration by the Proposer must be attached and 
enclosed as part of the proposal.
1-9 Selection Process: Responsive proposals will be evaluated by the Board. After 
review, up to three (3) proposers will be selected to present in-person oral 
presentations at a special meeting to be held by the Board on October 9, 2025. 
The criteria for selection is in the sole discretion of the board and will include, but 
not be limited to, factors described in the RFP. Nothing herein will prevent the 
Board from assigning work to any firm deemed responsive and responsible. The 
Board reserves the right to further negotiate any proposal, including fees, with the 
highest rated Proposer.

1-10 Public Records: Proposals become “public records” and shall be subject to public 
disclosure consistent with Chapter 119.07 Florida Statutes. Proposers must invoke 
any exemptions to disclosure provided by law in the response to the RFP and must 
identify the data or other materials to be protected, the reasons why such exemption

1-11 Public Entity Crimes: In accordance with Florida Statute 287.133, no award will

includes any natural person or entity, including predecessor or successor entities 
or an entity under the control of any natural person who is active in its management 
and who has been convicted of a public entity crime. 
1-12 Cone of Silence: The Cone of Silence is a prohibition on any communication, 
except for written correspondence, regarding a particular request for proposal, 
request for qualification, bid or any other competitive solicitation between:
(1) Any person or person’s representative seeking an award from such 
competitive solicitation; and
(2) Any member of the Board of Trustees of the City of Madison Police

For the purposes of this section, a person’s representative shall include but not be 
limited to the person’s employee, partner, officer, director, consultant, lobbyist, or 
any actual or potential subcontractor or consultant of the person. The cone of

1-18 Insurance: The awarded service provider shall obtain and maintain at it's own cost

be construed to be a breach of contract. The Board reserves the right to require

service provided by the Service Provider. 
Comprehensive General Liability Insurance coverage with limits of liability not less

than $1,000,000 Each Occurrence/$2,000,000 Aggregate. The Certificate of 
Insurance shall indicate an Occurrence Basis. The Plan shall be endorsed as an

Professional Liability (Errors & Omissions) - professional liability or equivalent

A copy of a current Certificate of Insurance should be included with your proposal.
1-19 In accordance with section 215.855, Florida Statutes, a contract between the Plan
and an investment adviser must require that any written communication made by 
the investment manager to a company in which such manager invests public funds 
on behalf of a governmental entity must include the following disclaimer in a 
conspicuous location if such communication discusses social, political, or 
ideological interests; subordinates the interests of the company’s shareholders to

the company’s shareholders: “The views and opinions expressed in this

of the people of the State of Florida.”

01259332-1 RFP No. 2025-__ - Investment Consulting and Management Services Page 12
4898-5945-2974, v. 1
PART II
NATURE OF SERVICES
2-1 Purpose and Scope of Work: The Board seeks proposals from qualified 
Investment Consulting Firms to provide general investment advice and counsel to 
the Board for the investment and management of funds for the City of Madison 
Police Officers’ and Firefighters Retirement System. 
The Plan was established by ordinance No. 2019-27 for the purpose of offering 
benefits to employees currently employed as Police Officers and Firefighters and 
retirees who were previously employed as Police Officers and Firefighters. The 
Plan is overseen by a Board of Trustees consisting of one Police Officer, one 
Firefighter, two City Commission appointees who are residents of the City of 
Madison and one appointee elected by majority of the previous four (4) trustees. 
Additionally, the plan administrator for the Plan is the Board or a designee thereof.
The total market value of the fund balance as of September 30, 2024 is 
approximately $7.07 million. In Fiscal Year 2024, there were payments to fifteen 
(15) pension recipients and contributions from twenty-one (21) actively employed 
members. The plan is approximately 80% funded. 
2-2 Minimum Requirements. Consultant must satisfy the following mandatory 
minimum requirements in order to have their Responses evaluated. By submitting 
a Response, Consultant warrants and represents that it satisfies these 
requirements. Failure to meet these requirements will potentially result in the 
Response not being evaluated and being rejected as non-responsive:
1. The Consultant/Firm shall provide current proof of all business licenses 
required by local, state, and federal law as applicable.
2. Minimum of five-year record of actual management/advisory of assets in the 
public pension fund sector.

01259332-1 RFP No. 2025-__ - Investment Consulting and Management Services Page 13
4898-5945-2974, v. 1
3. Be an investment advisor registered with the Securities and Exchange 
Commission under the investment Advisor’s Act of 1940. The Consultant 
shall be a fiduciary of the pension fund in accordance with the provisions of 
Florida Statutes, Section 112.656. The Consultant will not be expected to 
render legal, accounting, or actuarial service, or to prepare any such 
documents.
4. The consultant must be willing to accept the Fund’s required contractual 
terms and conditions as contained in this RFP.
2-3 Scope of Services Requested: Services to be provided by the Proposer(s) shall 
include, but not be limited to, the following:
1. Asset Allocation recommendation, to include portfolio optimization guidance 
for achieving a target rate or return range with reduced risk and volatility.
2. Evaluate the investment performance of the Fund Managers.
3. Provide written quarterly reports on investment activity, earnings and the value 
of the investment portfolio. The report provided to the Board should contain 
information which is typical or standard for such reports provided to the firm's 
other pension fund evaluation clients. At a minimum, the report should provide 
the following:
a. a comparison of actual returns with generally recognized indices;
b. separate detailed analysis for each investment manager’s 
performance and risk metrics and their corresponding effect on the 
portfolio as a whole;
c. total time-weighted returns for each asset class for the most recently 
completed quarter, 12 months, 3 years and 5 years (and 10 year if 
available);
d. Information presented in both table and graph form;

01259332-1 RFP No. 2025-__ - Investment Consulting and Management Services Page 14
4898-5945-2974, v. 1
e. Evaluation of investment performance relative to the fund’s written 
investment policies and guidelines and all major market indices and 
benchmarks
4. Provide recommendations to assist the Board in selecting a financially strong 
and adequately insured custodian, responsible for holding Plan assets. 
Proposer must be able to effectively coordinate with the custodian directly for 
any service needs to include withdrawal instructions on an ad hoc basis.
5. Work with Board to identify criteria for manager and/or fund inclusion.
6. Assist the Board with reviewing and, when appropriate, revising the Plan’s
investment policy, with manager selection and with asset allocation.
7. Provide manager, fund and general investment search and research. Advise 
when a manager should be placed on a watch list or probation and/or 
terminated.
8. Coordinate presentations, if requested, among fund managers.
9. Consult with Board on matters related to performance, news and 
developments in the capital markets, asset classes and/or funds that would 
make a material impact on the performance of the fund.
10. Attend quarterly Board meetings to present the investment performance 
report. 
11. Respond to Board, administrator and staff inquiries and requests for services 
in an appropriate and timely manner. 
12. Provide a database ranking for the total Plan returns and comparisons to 
appropriate indices on an annualized basis. The Consultant shall also provide 
this information for each Investment Manager/Mutual Fund.

01259332-1 RFP No. 2025-__ - Investment Consulting and Management Services Page 15
4898-5945-2974, v. 1
13. Monitor and ensure compliance with investment guidelines in the Investment 
Policy Statement, including rebalancing of assets, subject to approval by the
Board. Monitor material changes in regulations impacting investments and the 
management of public funds for pensions. 
14. Monitor performance of investment managers and prepare a report on a 
quarterly basis with updates on performance along with a comparison to both 
the actuarial assumed rate of return and an independent benchmark 
comprised of widely recognized and accepted indexes.
15. Identify a designated Consultant as well as a point of contact for service-related items for the Board.
16. Provide written acknowledgement of Fiduciary relationship to the Board and 
Plan.
17. Provide educational workshops on an as needed basis to support the 
development and growth of the current Board and/or Plan members.
18. Perform any other services not specifically listed that would normally be done 
periodically on a monthly, quarterly or annual basis.
2-3 Evaluation Criteria. Proposals will be evaluated by the Board in order to ascertain 
which Proposal best satisfies the scope of the services requested. Evaluation 
consideration will include, but not be limited to, the following:
1. Responsiveness of the Proposal in clearly stating an understanding of the 
work to be performed.
2. Technical ability of the Proposer(s) and consultant assigned to the case to 
perform consulting services.
3. Experience of Proposer(s) and assigned consultant.

01259332-1 RFP No. 2025-__ - Investment Consulting and Management Services Page 16
4898-5945-2974, v. 1
4. The fees and expenses are a significant factor. Fees and expenses will be a 
particularly important factor when all other evaluation criteria are relatively 
equal.
2-4 Proposal Content and Format: Proposals must provide complete information for 
each of the categories and/or questions below. Proposals which do not include the 
following information may be deemed non-responsive and may not be considered for the

I. Organization
a. Name of firm

i. Provide a detailed fee proposal. The fee proposal should address the

ADMINISTRATIVE MATTERS 
Type of Entity
The City of Austin Employees’ Retirement System (COAERS) is a single employer governmental 
defined benefit retirement system originally established in 1941 by City ordinance and governed 
since 1991 by Texas statute (Vernon’s Ann.Texas Civ.St. Art. 6243n). COAERS is qualified under 
Section 401(a) of the Internal Revenue Code. 
COAERS Board of Trustees
The COAERS Board of Trustees is vested with the statutory power and responsibility for the 
proper and effective general administration, management, and operation of the retirement 
system for the exclusive benefit of its present and future members and beneficiaries. The Board 
consists of 11 members comprised of City of Austin officials, employees, retirees, and citizens.
Participating Employers
Two employers participate in the Plan, the City of Austin Texas with over 17,000 active and 
deferred members and 7,100 retirees and the City of Austin Employees Retirement System 
staff with 38 active and deferred members and 13 retirees. 
Authority for Actuarial Services 
The COAERS Board of Trustees has statutory authority for the selection of an actuary. The 
statute states the Board of Trustees shall designate an actuary who shall be the technical 
advisor of the retirement board regarding the maintenance and operations of the fund but 
not an investment advisor or fiduciary with respect to any investments of the fund. The 
statute directs the actuary to perform valuations of the assets and liabilities of the fund.
Actuarial Determine Contribution Plan
COAERS is an actuarial determined contribution (ADC) rate plan in which, each year, the 
actuary determines the normal cost of the plan as a percentage of pay adjusting for the 
administrative expense and any liability layers established after December 31, 2022. The 
total normal cost of the plan isthen forecasted for the upcoming year. The forecasted normal 
cost is reduced by the employee contribution rate to yield the upcoming years’ employer 
contribution rate. The statutory requirements for the plan, including the determination of 
the ADC, can be found in the COAERS statutes at TX CIV ST Art 6243n.

SECTION ONE - FUNDING APPROACH 
1.1 Funding Approach in General
COAERS is an actuarial determined contribution (ADC) rate plan in which, each year, the actuary 
determines the normal cost of the plan as a percentage of pay adjusting for the administrative 
expense and amortization of any gain/loss layers (“liability layers) established after December 
31, 2022. The total normal cost of the plan is then forecasted for the upcoming year. The 
forecasted normal cost is reduced by the employee contribution rate to yield the upcoming years’ 
employer contribution rate. An existing amortization schedule of fixed payments, called Legacy 
Liability payments, has also been created to retire the plan’s Unfunded Actuarial Accrued 
Liability. The plan sponsor is required by law to make the required Legacy Liability payments in 
addition to the employer’s contribution each year. 
COAERS’ strategic funding objective is to meet the long-term pension obligations promised to 
all members of the plan. To meet this objective, COAERS has put in place a set of policies and 
legislative requirements to:
1. Establish a fixed payment schedule to pay off the Unfunded Actuarial Accrued Liability 
(UAAL) over a fixed, closed 30-year period, known as the Legacy Liability.
2. Conduct annual actuarial valuations, which include a Risk Sharing Valuation Study
(RSVS), to determine the ADC rate for the upcoming year for the employers participating 
in the plan (See TX CIV ST Art. 6243n for a full description of the state statute detailing 
the Risk Sharing Valuation Study).
3. Monitor the employer’s contribution rate relative to the expected future trajectory of 
the rate, known as a corridor midpoint.
4. If the employer portion of the ADC exceeds the corridor maximum (5% of pay above the 
corridor midpoint), take action to increase employee contributions up to the 2%
maximum, and discuss future changes to the Plan if the ADC exceeds the employer and 
employee maximums.
5. Periodically conduct Actuarial Experience Studies to review and adopt the assumptions 
and methods used to determine the cost of the promised benefits. State law requires 
Experience Studies to perform no less than every five years. The last Experience Study 
was conducted as of December 31, 2024.
1.2 Actuarial Determined Contribution
COAERS is an actuarially determined contribution (ADC) rate plan. The ADC is comprised of the 
normal cost and the administrative expense assumption adjusted for the amortization of any 
liability layers expressed as a percentage of pay. COAERS uses the Entry Age Normal actuarial 
cost method to develop the normal cost for each benefit component – retirement, termination, 
disability, etc. The administrative expense assumption is currently .70% of pay. 
In determining the future contribution rate, the actuary also determines if any adjustments are 
needed for gains or losses by way of additional liability layers. Such layers have already been 
established for 2023 and 2024 and will continue to be calculated each subsequent year. Future

10
actuarial losses are converted to a percentage of payroll, amortized, and the layer added to the 
normal cost. Future actuarial gains are converted to a percentage of payroll, amortized, and the 
layer subtracted from the normal cost. Based upon the result, the actuary then projects the 
normal cost for the future upcoming calendar year, and the employee contribution rate is 
subtracted to yield the employer contribution rate for the upcoming year.
In addition, a model of future expected employer contribution rates has also been established to 
help COAERS determine a range of future acceptable employer contribution rates. An Initial Risk 
Sharing Valuation Study (RSVS) was performed as of December 31, 2022 establishing a 
contribution rate corridor. The corridor has a midpoint which is the expected future trajectory 
of the employer contribution rate. Additionally, a minimum and a maximum employer 
contribution rate were also set at 5% of pay above and 5% of pay below the midpoint. This 
corridor provides COAERS with a range of possible future employer contribution rates. The 
contribution corridor is used to trigger important subsequent events. First, if the ADC would 
cause the employer contribution rate to exceed the corridor’s maximum contribution rate, then 
the employee contribution rate will have to increase accordingly. The increase would be added 
to the 10% current employee contribution rate up to an additional 2% of payroll to cover the 
shortfall. Second, if ADC exceeds the additional 2% of pay from the employees, then COAERS 
and the City of Austin must enter into discussions to come up with a plan to address the funding 
and the expense of the Plan. Finally, if the ADC is lower than the corridor midpoint, the employer 
contribution will remain at the corridor midpoint so long as the funded ratio is below 90%.

1.8 Experience Studies
COAERS believes that a periodic review of our actuarial assumptions is crucial to understanding 
and managing the cost of the benefits promised to members of COAERS. The use of outdated 
or inappropriate assumptions can result in understated costs which will lead to higher future
contribution rates; or overstated costs which place an unnecessary financial burden on the City 
of Austin and its employees. Accordingly, COAERS conducts experience studies every five years. 
During each experience study, each assumption is reviewed and compared to the actual 
experience of the plan with consideration of adding in a slight margin for adverse experience. 
Then the assumptions, as a whole, are reviewed for reasonableness and consistency. COAERS
recently reviewed its actuarial assumptions based on census data as of December 31, 2024. 
Certain key assumptions are listed below. A full discussion of the assumptions can be found in 
the Experience Study Report at www.coaers/RFP.

SECTION ONE - FUNDING APPROACH 
1.1 Funding Approach in General
COAERS is an actuarial determined contribution (ADC) rate plan in which, each year, the actuary 
determines the normal cost of the plan as a percentage of pay adjusting for the administrative 
expense and amortization of any gain/loss layers (“liability layers) established after December 
31, 2022. The total normal cost of the plan is then forecasted for the upcoming year. The 
forecasted normal cost is reduced by the employee contribution rate to yield the upcoming years’ 
employer contribution rate. An existing amortization schedule of fixed payments, called Legacy 
Liability payments, has also been created to retire the plan’s Unfunded Actuarial Accrued 
Liability. The plan sponsor is required by law to make the required Legacy Liability payments in 
addition to the employer’s contribution each year. 
COAERS’ strategic funding objective is to meet the long-term pension obligations promised to 
all members of the plan. To meet this objective, COAERS has put in place a set of policies and 
legislative requirements to:
1. Establish a fixed payment schedule to pay off the Unfunded Actuarial Accrued Liability 
(UAAL) over a fixed, closed 30-year period, known as the Legacy Liability.
2. Conduct annual actuarial valuations, which include a Risk Sharing Valuation Study
(RSVS), to determine the ADC rate for the upcoming year for the employers participating 
in the plan (See TX CIV ST Art. 6243n for a full description of the state statute detailing 
the Risk Sharing Valuation Study).
3. Monitor the employer’s contribution rate relative to the expected future trajectory of 
the rate, known as a corridor midpoint.
4. If the employer portion of the ADC exceeds the corridor maximum (5% of pay above the 
corridor midpoint), take action to increase employee contributions up to the 2%
maximum, and discuss future changes to the Plan if the ADC exceeds the employer and 
employee maximums.
5. Periodically conduct Actuarial Experience Studies to review and adopt the assumptions 
and methods used to determine the cost of the promised benefits. State law requires 
Experience Studies to perform no less than every five years. The last Experience Study 
was conducted as of December 31, 2024.
1.2 Actuarial Determined Contribution
COAERS is an actuarially determined contribution (ADC) rate plan. The ADC is comprised of the 
normal cost and the administrative expense assumption adjusted for the amortization of any 
liability layers expressed as a percentage of pay. COAERS uses the Entry Age Normal actuarial 
cost method to develop the normal cost for each benefit component – retirement, termination, 
disability, etc. The administrative expense assumption is currently .70% of pay. 
In determining the future contribution rate, the actuary also determines if any adjustments are 
needed for gains or losses by way of additional liability layers. Such layers have already been 
established for 2023 and 2024 and will continue to be calculated each subsequent year. Future

10
actuarial losses are converted to a percentage of payroll, amortized, and the layer added to the 
normal cost. Future actuarial gains are converted to a percentage of payroll, amortized, and the 
layer subtracted from the normal cost. Based upon the result, the actuary then projects the 
normal cost for the future upcoming calendar year, and the employee contribution rate is 
subtracted to yield the employer contribution rate for the upcoming year.
In addition, a model of future expected employer contribution rates has also been established to 
help COAERS determine a range of future acceptable employer contribution rates. An Initial Risk 
Sharing Valuation Study (RSVS) was performed as of December 31, 2022 establishing a 
contribution rate corridor. The corridor has a midpoint which is the expected future trajectory 
of the employer contribution rate. Additionally, a minimum and a maximum employer 
contribution rate were also set at 5% of pay above and 5% of pay below the midpoint. This 
corridor provides COAERS with a range of possible future employer contribution rates. The 
contribution corridor is used to trigger important subsequent events. First, if the ADC would 
cause the employer contribution rate to exceed the corridor’s maximum contribution rate, then 
the employee contribution rate will have to increase accordingly. The increase would be added 
to the 10% current employee contribution rate up to an additional 2% of payroll to cover the 
shortfall. Second, if ADC exceeds the additional 2% of pay from the employees, then COAERS 
and the City of Austin must enter into discussions to come up with a plan to address the funding 
and the expense of the Plan. Finally, if the ADC is lower than the corridor midpoint, the employer 
contribution will remain at the corridor midpoint so long as the funded ratio is below 90%.

Gains and losses realized after 2022, create new amortization layers adjusting the normal cost

As of March 31, 2025, COAERS held investments with fair value totaling $3.5 billion. The 
Board has found it prudent to diversify both across and within the major asset classes to
construct a portfolio that delivers strong compound returns on a long-term, risk-adjusted 
basis. The Board recently adopted a new strategic asset allocation as shown below. Note 
however, that it is expected to take some time to ramp up the private market’s elements of 
the new strategic asset allocation.

12
Investments are made with care, skill, prudence, and diligence under the circumstances then 
prevailing that a prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters would 
use in the conduct of an enterprise of a like character and with like aims. Funds of COAERS are 
invested solely in the interest of the membership and their beneficiaries, and for the exclusive 
purpose of providing benefits to such membership and their beneficiaries while defraying 
reasonable expenses of administering COAERS. 
The Board of Trustees has established an Investment Policy Statement and related guidelines for 
the administration of the investment program. Moreover, an Investment Committee has been 
chartered to assist the Board with research, recommendations, and monitoring of the investment 
portfolio. Investment consulting services are provided by the Meketa Investment Group and 
COAERS employs four professionals to oversee day-to-day implementation activities of the
investment portfolio.

COAERS believes that a periodic review of our actuarial assumptions is crucial to understanding 
and managing the cost of the benefits promised to members of COAERS. The use of outdated 
or inappropriate assumptions can result in understated costs which will lead to higher future
contribution rates; or overstated costs which place an unnecessary financial burden on the City 
of Austin and its employees. Accordingly, COAERS conducts experience studies every five years. 
During each experience study, each assumption is reviewed and compared to the actual 
experience of the plan with consideration of adding in a slight margin for adverse experience.

2.1 Personnel
All services provided for the scope of services described herein must be performed under the 
direct supervision of a Supervising Actuary who have been regularly engaged in the business of 
providing actuarial services for at least 10 years and must have the designation of either an 
Associate or Fellow of the Society of Actuaries and/or Member of the American Academy of 
Actuaries. The Supervising Actuary must approve all the work provided to COAERS. The 
Respondent will identify the Supervising Actuary in its response.
2.2 Annual Actuarial Valuation (Including a Risk Sharing Valuation Study)
a) Description of Work: 
1) Measurements using the following actuarial methods:
i) Entry Age Normal Cost method will be used to allocate the cost of accruing benefits 
as a level percentage of pay over the period from the member’s entry into the plan 
until termination or retirement;
ii) Five-year smoothing method asset method which recognizes 20% of the differences 
between expected and actual investment income in the current and each 
subsequent year, with offsetting unrecognized gains and losses immediately
recognized; and a
iii) A declining 30-year amortization period to determine the payments on new liability 
layers until reaching 20-years, thereafter, using closed 20-year layers. The aggregate 
funding period for the system is the weighted average of the amortization layers. 
The goal is to eliminate negative amortization as soon as possible, but negative 
amortization is expected to continue until the Legacy Liability payoff schedule 
reaches 20 years.
2) The RSVS will include:
i) An Executive Summary;
ii) Discussion of the following at a minimum:
(1) Actuarially Determined Contribution Corridor;
(2) Calculated Actuarially Determined City Contribution Rate;
(3) Projection of Remaining Legacy Liability and Legacy Liability Payments;
(4) Liability (Gain)/Loss Layers;
(5) Funded status of the Plan;
(6) Change in Assets;
(7) Actuarial Gains and Losses; 
(8) An assessment of Disclosure of Risk Associated with Measuring Pension 
Obligations
(9) Disclosure of Actuarial Methods and Assumptions

15
(10) Actuarial and Statistical Tables;
(11) Definition of Terms; and 
iii) Other requirements mandated by the Actuarial Standards of Practice (American 
Academy of Actuaries) and/or the Government Accounting Standards Board.
(b) Prework. Respondent will load, review, and reconcile census data provided for the 
valuations. COAERS will provide the Respondent with data and information to perform 
valuations and other services, provided the data is available and in COAERS’ records. 
Respondent must provide a secure method of transferring electronic information. Contractor 
will review the census data and test it for reasonableness disclosing any irregularities to the 
COAERS staff. If Respondent omits information or categorizes information differently than in 
original census files, vendor must reconcile and disclose that reconciliation to COAERS prior to 
the issuance of the valuation. Respondents should review the census data formats located at 
www.coaers.org/RFP for the file format and description of the current census data files. 
Respondent must be able to receive and use the existing files and formatting. 
(c) Travel & Formal Presentation. Respondent will provide one in-person presentation 
discussing the Actuarial Valuation including the Risk Sharing Valuation for the COAERS Benefits 
& Services Committee one time per year in Austin, Texas.

I. Introduction
The San Diego City Employees' Retirement System (SDCERS) is requesting proposals 
from general investment consultants to provide comprehensive pension fund investment 
consulting services. SDCERS is seeking proposals from independent general 
investment consultants who have consulting experience in the public pension fund area. 
Firms are invited to participate in an evaluation process to further represent their 
capabilities of rendering the following consultant services:
Investment Policy
Asset Allocation and Portfolio Oversight
Investment Manager Oversight
Performance Measurement
Training, Education and Client Service 
See section V. for further details on each service area.
II. Proposal Participation, Completion and Submission Procedures
General Investment Consulting firms wishing to respond to this RFP must meet the 
following minimum qualifications as of January 1, 2027:
A. Mandatory Requirements Certification and Minimum Requirements
SDCERS will accept proposals from firms that meet the minimum requirements listed 
below. The proposing firm must complete the Mandatory Requirements Certification 
(attached as Attachment A) and submit it with the cover letter.
1. The consulting firm must be a registered advisor under the Investment Company Act 
of 1940. Please include copies of ADV I and II (with schedules) as Exhibit A. 
2. The consulting firm must have substantial experience advising multi-billion public 
pension plan retirement systems. 
3. The consulting firm must have at least five (5) years of continuous experience in 
performing general investment consulting for large institutional clients (endowments 
and foundations), corporate pension plans or tax-exempt public funds.

SDCERS General Investment Consultant RFP – August
2026 Page 4
4. The consulting firm must be able to maintain a satisfactory data processing interface 
with SDCERS’ custodian, State Street Bank, on-line connection or other electronic 
means, at the firm’s expense, for the purposes of compiling all required reviews and 
reports.
5. The consulting firm must agree to disclose all potential, current conflicts of interest as 
well as potential conflicts as they might occur and annually disclose all sources of 
revenue from sources and affiliations other than investment consulting.
6. The consulting firm must agree to abide by SDCERS’ Conflict of Interest policy and 
Placement Agent Disclosure Policy. These policies can be found in the link labeled 
Board Policies on SDCERS’ website at https://www.sdcers.gov/resources/governing-documents. If any material conflict of interest is found during the duration of the 
contract, the consulting firm will notify SDCERS’ Chief Investment Officer.
7. The consulting firm must be directly responsible for the management of the account, 
and all personnel responsible for working on the account must be employees of the 
firm.
8. The consulting firm must not have, nor potentially have, a material conflict of interest 
to include, but not limited to: SDCERS’ Board, Staff, Actuary, External Auditor, 
Investment Managers, or other consultants.
9. The consulting firm must carry Errors and Omissions coverage and other insuranc e 
coverage as discussed in Section V. Insurance Requirements.
10. The consulting firm must have its principal place of business within the United States 
and be subject to service of process in the United States.
11. All minimum qualifications must be met by January 1, 2027.

All responses to this RFP become the property of SDCERS and will be kept confidential 
until a recommendation for award of a contract has been announced. Thereafter, 
submittals are subject to public inspection and disclosure under the law, including but not 
limited to, the California Public Records Act (Gov. Code §§ 7920.000 et seq.) In the event 
SDCERS receives a request for a copy or inspection of any proposal submitted pursuant 
to this RFP, SDCERS will notify the Proposer, the individual who is authorized to bind the 
consulting firm, before providing a response. There are specific exemptions to the Public

2026 Page 5
Records Act, however, it is the responsibility of the Proposer to assert and seek a judicial 
determination as to any right of confidentiality that may exist. SDCERS will not makethat 
assertion on behalf of the Proposer. Absent a judicial determination that the documents 
are exempt from disclosure, they will be subject to public inspection. Submission of a 
proposal constitutes a complete waiver of any claims whatsoever against SDCERS,

A. Background Information
The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS) was created by the Anchorage 
Municipal Assembly by ordinance in 1977 (AO No.77-205; AO No. 84-69; AO No. 2000-
65, § 3, 4-18-00). Police and fire employees hired July 1, 1968, or later retroactively 
became members in the retirement plan. 
The system is comprised of three retirement plans including a surplus benefit plan, all of 
which were created for the purpose of encouraging qualified personnel to enter and remain 
in the service of the Municipality of Anchorage as police officers and firefighters through 
the establishment of a system of retirement, disability and death benefits for members, and
their beneficiaries. The retirement plans are closed with Plan I closing to new members 
effective June 30, 1977, Plan II closing to new members effective April 17, 1984, and Plan
III closing to new members effective May 24, 1994, for new command police and fire, July 
17, 1994, for union firefighters and all new union police officers October 5, 1994.
A nine-member Board of Trustees governs APFRS. The Board has sole and exclusive 
fiduciary responsibility over the assets of the retirement system. The Board has sole and 
exclusive responsibility to administer APFRS in a manner that will assure prompt delivery
of benefits and related services to the members and their beneficiaries.
The APFRS Director has the responsibility for the overall management and administration 
of the system in accordance with the direction, policy and goals set by the Board and 
Anchorage Municipal Code. Reporting to the Director is a staff with the primary
responsibility to assist the Director to carry out these policies and goals.
An annual actuarial valuation commissioned by the Board determines contributions into the 
APFRS Plans. The Retirement System is also subject to an annual independent audit
commissioned by the Board. The results of the actuarial valuation and audit are provided
to the Board, Municipal Executives, and Municipal Assembly.

ANCHORAGE POLICE AND FIRE RETIREMENT SYSTEM 
STATEMENT OF INVESTMENT POLICY
FOREWORD
The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS) was created by the 
Anchorage Municipal Assembly by ordinance in 1977 (AO No.77-205; AO No. 84-69; 
AO No. 2000-65, § 3, 4-18-00). Police and Fire employees hired July 1, 1968 or later 
retroactively became members in the retirement plan. 
The system is comprised of three retirement plans, all of which were created for the 
purpose of encouraging qualified personnel to enter and remain in the service of the 
Municipality of Anchorage as police officers and firefighters through the establishment 
of a system of retirement, disability and death benefits for members, and their 
beneficiaries. The retirement plans are closed with Plan I closing to new members 
effective June 30, 1977, Plan II closing to new members effective April 17, 1984, and 
Plan III closing to new members effective May 24, 1994 for new command police and 
fire, July 17, 1994 for union firefighters and all new union police officers
October 5, 1994. 
A nine member Board of Trustees governs APFRS. The Board has sole and exclusive 
fiduciary responsibility over the assets of the retirement system. The Board has the sole 
and exclusive responsibility to administer APFRS in a manner that will assure prompt 
delivery of benefits and related services to the members and their beneficiaries.
The APFRS Director has the responsibility for the overall management and 
administration of the system in accordance with the direction, policy and goals set by the 
Board and Anchorage Municipal Code. Reporting to the Director is a staff with the 
primary responsibility to assist the Director to carry out these policies and goals.
An annual actuarial valuation commissioned by the Board determines contributions into 
the APFRS Plans. The growth of the Fund results from a combination of employer and 
employee contributions plus investment gains, less the combination of administrative 
costs, investment expenses, and benefit payments. The Retirement System is also subject 
to an annual outside audit commissioned by the Board. The results of the actuarial 
valuation and audit are provided to the Board, Municipal Executives, and Assembly.

3 
THE PURPOSE OF THE INVESTMENT POLICY AND OBJECTIVES:
1. Articulate the Board’s views on APFRS’ investment objectives and risk tolerance 
for the investment portfolio. 
2. Establish performance standards to measure the progress towards achieving the 
objectives.
3. Formulate the Board’s policies and guidelines on: a) asset allocation and 
diversification of investments; b) allowable investments; c) rebalancing; d) 
implementing policy-based initiatives; e) monitoring and evaluating the 
performance and risk of the investment portfolio; and f) investment manager 
selection and termination.
I.
1. 
INVESTMENT GOAL:
Provide for present and future benefit payments including increased benefits should reserves 
exceed 116%. The overall purpose is to invest pension assets, solely in the interest of providing
benefits to the members and their beneficiaries, attempting to minimize the employer and 
employee contributions and defraying administrative costs. The investment of the fund assets 
made in accordance with the investment policy described herein are expected to accomplish the 
goal of maintaining adequate funding of AFPRS’ liabilities over time.
The goal of the Board is to design an investment portfolio that will achieve an actuarial rate of 
return assumption of 6.90%. 
2. Make Prudent Investments – With care, skill, prudence and diligence the Board 
will strive to produce an investment return based on levels of liquidity and 
investment risk that are prudent and reasonable under present circumstances. 
Such circumstances may change over time.
3. Diversify the Assets – The Board will diversify the investments of the Fund to 
maximize the investment return within acceptable investment risk. 
4. Establish policy and review process – Annually, APFRS will conduct a 
formal review of its Investment Policy and will consider long term financial 
projections prepared by the Investment Consultant. 
II. INVESTMENT PHILOSOPHY:
In general, research has shown that the level of investment return is related to the 
corresponding level of investment risk. To achieve the actuarial target earning 
goal, the Board has adopted a long-term strategic asset allocation plan. APFRS 
will utilize some level of active investment management strategy to provide 
additional return required to achieve the target earnings rate. The Board strives

to seek a balance between the certainties of obtaining a set return over time with
the risks inherent in higher investment returns. The Board may employ lower 
cost and lower risk strategies to achieve its stated earnings goals 
III. INVESTMENT OBJECTIVES:
It is in the best interest of the Retirement System that investment objectives be 
established by the Board for the total fund and for each investment manager. It is 
clearly understood that these objectives are to be viewed over the long-term and 
have been established after full consideration of all factors set out in this 
Statement of Investment Policy (“SIP”). The investment objectives are as 
follows: 
A. Total Fund Investment Objectives
1. To achieve a minimum return of 5.0% in excess of the U.S. City 
Average, All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) as reported by the Bureau of 
Labor Statistics. However, the return shall be no less than the stated 
return the actuary utilizes in determining future normal benefit costs.
2. Exceed the return of a custom index, based on the target asset mix 
specified in Section V.D.
3. The Board shall strive to achieve a level of 116% funding (the 
Contingency Reserve) of the retirement system’s pension benefit 
liability in each Plan over time. Also, in each Plan, the Board will 
annually set aside 25% of any identified surpluses as an additional 
contingency reserve as required by Municipal Code. The Board has 
the authority with a simple majority vote to distribute the surplus in 
accordance with AMC 3.85. 
4. Surpluses above the additional contingency reserve may be available
for enhanced benefits only upon concurrence and recommendation of 
the Board's actuary and approval by a Super-Majority of the 
Retirement Board and by ordinance approved by the Anchorage 
Assembly. 
B. The Investment Managers Agreement may also contain additional 
investment performance objectives and goals for performance monitoring. 
IV. BOARD AND CONTRACTOR RESPONSIBILITIES:
The Board, under the Anchorage Municipal Code Chapter 3.85, is responsible for 
the establishment of investment policies that guide investment of the Anchorage 
Police and Fire Retirement System assets. As such:
A. The Board Shall determine the appropriate investment policies by 
considering the implications of a wide range of financial assumptions and

investment risk; 
B. The Board is the sole authority for hiring, retaining, and releasing 
managers, investment consultant and the master custodian; 
C. The managers shall be responsible to the Board for carrying out the 
Board’s investment goals, objectives and policies; 
D. The managers are accorded full discretion, within investment policy 
limits, to select individual securities and diversify assets under their 
control. Manager discretion may also be limited by the terms of the 
investment management agreement between the System and the 
manager;
E. The master custodian shall be responsible for safekeeping assets under the 
master custodian’s supervision and shall be responsible for administering 
any Securities Lending Agreement between the Board and the bank; 
F. The Director shall be responsible for implementing the Board’s 
investment policies, monitoring the managers and master custodian, and 
deploying assets within the established asset allocation parameters.
G. The Investment Consultant shall review and evaluate the performance of 
investment managers for APFRS and provide written quarterly reports and 
advice to the Board. The Investment Consultant shall attend regular 
periodic meetings and make oral presentations regarding the investment 
managers’ performance during each period. The Investment Consultant 
shall conduct an annual review of APFRS investment objectives, 
guidelines and procedures and, if necessary, make recommendations for 
amendments thereto. When necessary, assist the Board with interim 
changes to the System’s Asset Allocation Policy when managers are either 
added or deleted.
V. INVESTMENT POLICIES:
A. Actuarially Required Return
The assets of the Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System shall be 
invested to provide an actuarially required return on investment within
acceptable risk parameters, as specified in V.C.4 below, (Acceptable 
Investment Risk). 
B. Prudent Person Rule

The Board of Trustees is by law collectively and individually, considered 
to be fiduciaries of the System and shall discharge its responsibilities 
solely in the interest of the members and beneficiaries of the System for 
the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to the members and their 
beneficiaries and to defray the reasonable expenses of the System. The 
Trustees shall exercise those fiduciary responsibilities with the care, skill, 
prudence and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a 
prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters 
would use in the conduct of an enterprise of a similar character and with 
similar aims.
C. Asset Allocation Factors
The Board shall carefully consider the following factors in establishing a 
long-term asset allocation program:
1. Retirement System Characteristics:
a. The system is a public system with tax-exempt status, and 
investments shall be made in a fiduciary responsible manner for 
the benefit of the membership.
b. It is understood by the Board that member and municipal 
contributions may be required from time to time. However, the 
primary source of revenue for benefit payments is from investment 
earnings on the Retirement System’s assets.
c. Plan member demographics and nature of the Plans’ liabilities will 
be considered when developing an investment strategy. 
Additionally with APFRS being a closed system, the Board will 
take into consideration time horizons and invest in more 
conservative investments over time. 
2. Liquidity Requirements:
The System’s assets shall be structured to meet the liquidity 
requirements to pay benefits in a timely manner. Accordingly, the 
managers should be prepared to provide assets to meet liquidity 
requirements as the need arises. In addition, investment manager fees 
benefit payments and expenses will, at the discretion of the Director, 
be deducted directly from all portfolios. It is important that each 
manager maintain sufficient liquidity to cover these periodic 
withdrawals.
3. Quarterly Allocation Rebalancing:
The Director, in conjunction with the Fund’s Investment Consultant, 
will review the asset allocation quarterly and compare it to the 
recommended target allocation. When one particular manager’s 
portfolio is over-weighted versus their target allocation, the Director, 
after coordinating with the Investment Consultant, may reallocate the

“overage” required by the allocation model and report that activity to 
the Board at the next ensuing meeting. An ongoing exception is 
made for alternative asset classes, which may differ from the target 
ranges outlined for periods of time, due to the illiquid nature of the 
asset classes. In the event the existing allocation is within the
maximum/minimum guidelines (see V. D. below) no action may be 
taken.
The Board will review the overall fund allocation of assets at their 
annual review meeting. Significantly over-weighted asset classes may 
be cut back at that time, particularly those which fall outside the 
guideline allocations. Otherwise, the Board will rely on the advice of 
the Investment Consultant for changes to weightings or to the Asset 
Allocation model.
4. Acceptable Investment Risk:
The aggregate risk level appropriate for the retirement system is 
specified in this investment policy statement, which reflects the Fund’s 
characteristics, and liquidity requirements, keeping in mind the 
fiduciary purpose for which the assets are accumulated. The 
acceptable risk level is specified in Section V. D.
5. Asset Allocation Studies:
Periodic asset allocation studies may be considered annually by the 
Board which will:
a. Develop a long range rationale to guide the deployment of 
contributions and assets;
b. Identify appropriate expected risk/return parameters for the 
investment of System assets; and
c. Reassess the current investment policy as it pertains to the 
relationship between the System’s assets and liabilities.
6. Capital Market Assumptions:
Capital market assumptions are reviewed annually by the Board and the 
Investment Consultant. 
D. Asset Allocation Program
After careful consideration of the above referenced asset allocation 
factors, the Board has established a long-term asset allocation program 
that leads to an appropriate asset mix, realistic investment objectives and 
relevant investment constraints, as summarized on the next page:

(b) credit quality; (c) restricted transactions; and (d) exceptions.

(1) No individual security of the portfolio shall
constitute more than the greater of 5% or the

plus 2%. Other exceptions to this provision may be

investment, and shall constitute no more than 20% of 
the market value of the assets controlled by a 
manager.
(3) Exchange listed derivatives may be included in a

holding these securities in their portfolio, the likely
portfolio percentage allocation to derivatives and a

investments. Collateralized mortgage securities or
mortgage-backed securities are authorized by the Board,

The managers shall purchase or sell securities through those firms 
offering the best price and execution. The Board reserves the right
to institute a Brokerage Recapture Program or to use the services of 
a “Transition Management” brokerage firm if the Board believes 
this is in the best interest. The decision to use a third party will be
based on advice and recommendations from the Board’s Investment 
Consultant.

12
G. MANAGER PERFORMANCE STANDARDS
Over the long-term (as defined in the following paragraph) each manager retained 
to actively manage a portfolio will be expected to outperform on a net of fee basis 
an appropriately defined and mutually agreed upon market index and to perform 
(gross of fees) in the top two-fifths (2/5) of managers with similar investment 
styles as measured by one of the prevailing investment performance measurement 
services.
The time period for measuring manager performance is a market cycle or three to 
five years, whichever period is shorter. However, if a manager experiences 
significant organizational changes and/or its performance falls significantly below 
market averages, the performance of a group of managers of similar style, and its 
individual performance objectives prior to completion of a market cycle, then the 
manager’s performance will be evaluated over a shorter time horizon. Over the 
life of the portfolio, each manager is expected to maintain a portfolio with 
consistent fundamental portfolio characteristics.
H. MONITORING AND EVALUATING MANAGER PERFORMANCE
The monitoring and evaluating the total fund and individual managers’ 
performance will be performed by an Investment Consultant. The objective and 
purpose of this monitoring is to maintain adequate control over the System’s 
assets and the managers without stifling their initiative. The Board shall conduct 
a formal evaluation of each manager’s performance quarterly. These evaluations 
will focus on adherence to investment policies and the opportunities available in 
the investment markets. Particular attention will be directed to evaluating 
performance relative to risk; this will be achieved by comparing individual 
managers and total Fund performance on a risk-adjusted basis. It is believed that 
the performance expectations set forth in this SIP are reasonable and consistent in 
the long run. 
Actions to be taken as a result of performance reviews will be in accordance with 
the Retirement Board’s Investment Monitoring and Transition Process Procedure 
in Exhibit A. Notwithstanding the performance measures in Exhibit A, the Board 
retains the authority to terminate any manager whenever it is deemed, in the 
Board’s exercise of its fiduciary duty, to be in the best interest of the System and 
its participants.

13
I. ADOPTION
This Statement of Investment Policy is adopted effective April 18, 2000, the date 
the revised Anchorage Municipal Code, Chapter 3.85 (Re-established), was 
approved by the Municipal Assembly. (See the “Document History” on the 
attached Page.)
J. APPROVAL
This latest revision to the Statement of Investment Policy is approved by a super-majority vote of the Retirement Board at the meeting held on August 16, 2023.

the part of Consultant or its officers, directors, employees, affiliates, agents, servants,

I. TERM AND TERMINATION

The parties agree that services under this contract shall commence on January

EXHIBIT 3
Statement of Investment Policy

ANCHORAGE POLICE AND FIRE RETIREMENT SYSTEM 
STATEMENT OF INVESTMENT POLICY
FOREWORD
The Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System (APFRS) was created by the 
Anchorage Municipal Assembly by ordinance in 1977 (AO No.77-205; AO No. 84-69; 
AO No. 2000-65, § 3, 4-18-00). Police and Fire employees hired July 1, 1968 or later 
retroactively became members in the retirement plan. 
The system is comprised of three retirement plans, all of which were created for the 
purpose of encouraging qualified personnel to enter and remain in the service of the 
Municipality of Anchorage as police officers and firefighters through the establishment 
of a system of retirement, disability and death benefits for members, and their 
beneficiaries. The retirement plans are closed with Plan I closing to new members 
effective June 30, 1977, Plan II closing to new members effective April 17, 1984, and 
Plan III closing to new members effective May 24, 1994 for new command police and 
fire, July 17, 1994 for union firefighters and all new union police officers
October 5, 1994. 
A nine member Board of Trustees governs APFRS. The Board has sole and exclusive 
fiduciary responsibility over the assets of the retirement system. The Board has the sole 
and exclusive responsibility to administer APFRS in a manner that will assure prompt 
delivery of benefits and related services to the members and their beneficiaries.
The APFRS Director has the responsibility for the overall management and 
administration of the system in accordance with the direction, policy and goals set by the 
Board and Anchorage Municipal Code. Reporting to the Director is a staff with the 
primary responsibility to assist the Director to carry out these policies and goals.
An annual actuarial valuation commissioned by the Board determines contributions into 
the APFRS Plans. The growth of the Fund results from a combination of employer and 
employee contributions plus investment gains, less the combination of administrative 
costs, investment expenses, and benefit payments. The Retirement System is also subject 
to an annual outside audit commissioned by the Board. The results of the actuarial 
valuation and audit are provided to the Board, Municipal Executives, and Assembly.

3 
THE PURPOSE OF THE INVESTMENT POLICY AND OBJECTIVES:
1. Articulate the Board’s views on APFRS’ investment objectives and risk tolerance 
for the investment portfolio. 
2. Establish performance standards to measure the progress towards achieving the 
objectives.
3. Formulate the Board’s policies and guidelines on: a) asset allocation and 
diversification of investments; b) allowable investments; c) rebalancing; d) 
implementing policy-based initiatives; e) monitoring and evaluating the 
performance and risk of the investment portfolio; and f) investment manager 
selection and termination.
I.
1. 
INVESTMENT GOAL:
Provide for present and future benefit payments including increased benefits should reserves 
exceed 116%. The overall purpose is to invest pension assets, solely in the interest of providing
benefits to the members and their beneficiaries, attempting to minimize the employer and 
employee contributions and defraying administrative costs. The investment of the fund assets 
made in accordance with the investment policy described herein are expected to accomplish the 
goal of maintaining adequate funding of AFPRS’ liabilities over time.
The goal of the Board is to design an investment portfolio that will achieve an actuarial rate of 
return assumption of 6.90%. 
2. Make Prudent Investments – With care, skill, prudence and diligence the Board 
will strive to produce an investment return based on levels of liquidity and 
investment risk that are prudent and reasonable under present circumstances. 
Such circumstances may change over time.
3. Diversify the Assets – The Board will diversify the investments of the Fund to 
maximize the investment return within acceptable investment risk. 
4. Establish policy and review process – Annually, APFRS will conduct a 
formal review of its Investment Policy and will consider long term financial 
projections prepared by the Investment Consultant. 
II. INVESTMENT PHILOSOPHY:
In general, research has shown that the level of investment return is related to the 
corresponding level of investment risk. To achieve the actuarial target earning 
goal, the Board has adopted a long-term strategic asset allocation plan. APFRS 
will utilize some level of active investment management strategy to provide 
additional return required to achieve the target earnings rate. The Board strives

to seek a balance between the certainties of obtaining a set return over time with
the risks inherent in higher investment returns. The Board may employ lower 
cost and lower risk strategies to achieve its stated earnings goals 
III. INVESTMENT OBJECTIVES:
It is in the best interest of the Retirement System that investment objectives be 
established by the Board for the total fund and for each investment manager. It is 
clearly understood that these objectives are to be viewed over the long-term and 
have been established after full consideration of all factors set out in this 
Statement of Investment Policy (“SIP”). The investment objectives are as 
follows: 
A. Total Fund Investment Objectives
1. To achieve a minimum return of 5.0% in excess of the U.S. City 
Average, All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) as reported by the Bureau of 
Labor Statistics. However, the return shall be no less than the stated 
return the actuary utilizes in determining future normal benefit costs.
2. Exceed the return of a custom index, based on the target asset mix 
specified in Section V.D.
3. The Board shall strive to achieve a level of 116% funding (the 
Contingency Reserve) of the retirement system’s pension benefit 
liability in each Plan over time. Also, in each Plan, the Board will 
annually set aside 25% of any identified surpluses as an additional 
contingency reserve as required by Municipal Code. The Board has 
the authority with a simple majority vote to distribute the surplus in 
accordance with AMC 3.85. 
4. Surpluses above the additional contingency reserve may be available
for enhanced benefits only upon concurrence and recommendation of 
the Board's actuary and approval by a Super-Majority of the 
Retirement Board and by ordinance approved by the Anchorage 
Assembly. 
B. The Investment Managers Agreement may also contain additional 
investment performance objectives and goals for performance monitoring. 
IV. BOARD AND CONTRACTOR RESPONSIBILITIES:
The Board, under the Anchorage Municipal Code Chapter 3.85, is responsible for 
the establishment of investment policies that guide investment of the Anchorage 
Police and Fire Retirement System assets. As such:
A. The Board Shall determine the appropriate investment policies by 
considering the implications of a wide range of financial assumptions and

investment risk; 
B. The Board is the sole authority for hiring, retaining, and releasing 
managers, investment consultant and the master custodian; 
C. The managers shall be responsible to the Board for carrying out the 
Board’s investment goals, objectives and policies; 
D. The managers are accorded full discretion, within investment policy 
limits, to select individual securities and diversify assets under their 
control. Manager discretion may also be limited by the terms of the 
investment management agreement between the System and the 
manager;
E. The master custodian shall be responsible for safekeeping assets under the 
master custodian’s supervision and shall be responsible for administering 
any Securities Lending Agreement between the Board and the bank; 
F. The Director shall be responsible for implementing the Board’s 
investment policies, monitoring the managers and master custodian, and 
deploying assets within the established asset allocation parameters.
G. The Investment Consultant shall review and evaluate the performance of 
investment managers for APFRS and provide written quarterly reports and 
advice to the Board. The Investment Consultant shall attend regular 
periodic meetings and make oral presentations regarding the investment 
managers’ performance during each period. The Investment Consultant 
shall conduct an annual review of APFRS investment objectives, 
guidelines and procedures and, if necessary, make recommendations for 
amendments thereto. When necessary, assist the Board with interim 
changes to the System’s Asset Allocation Policy when managers are either 
added or deleted.
V. INVESTMENT POLICIES:
A. Actuarially Required Return
The assets of the Anchorage Police and Fire Retirement System shall be 
invested to provide an actuarially required return on investment within
acceptable risk parameters, as specified in V.C.4 below, (Acceptable 
Investment Risk). 
B. Prudent Person Rule

The Board of Trustees is by law collectively and individually, considered 
to be fiduciaries of the System and shall discharge its responsibilities 
solely in the interest of the members and beneficiaries of the System for 
the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to the members and their 
beneficiaries and to defray the reasonable expenses of the System. The 
Trustees shall exercise those fiduciary responsibilities with the care, skill, 
prudence and diligence under the circumstances then prevailing that a 
prudent person acting in a like capacity and familiar with such matters 
would use in the conduct of an enterprise of a similar character and with 
similar aims.
C. Asset Allocation Factors
The Board shall carefully consider the following factors in establishing a 
long-term asset allocation program:
1. Retirement System Characteristics:
a. The system is a public system with tax-exempt status, and 
investments shall be made in a fiduciary responsible manner for 
the benefit of the membership.
b. It is understood by the Board that member and municipal 
contributions may be required from time to time. However, the 
primary source of revenue for benefit payments is from investment 
earnings on the Retirement System’s assets.
c. Plan member demographics and nature of the Plans’ liabilities will 
be considered when developing an investment strategy. 
Additionally with APFRS being a closed system, the Board will 
take into consideration time horizons and invest in more 
conservative investments over time. 
2. Liquidity Requirements:
The System’s assets shall be structured to meet the liquidity 
requirements to pay benefits in a timely manner. Accordingly, the 
managers should be prepared to provide assets to meet liquidity 
requirements as the need arises. In addition, investment manager fees 
benefit payments and expenses will, at the discretion of the Director, 
be deducted directly from all portfolios. It is important that each 
manager maintain sufficient liquidity to cover these periodic 
withdrawals.
3. Quarterly Allocation Rebalancing:
The Director, in conjunction with the Fund’s Investment Consultant, 
will review the asset allocation quarterly and compare it to the 
recommended target allocation. When one particular manager’s 
portfolio is over-weighted versus their target allocation, the Director, 
after coordinating with the Investment Consultant, may reallocate the

“overage” required by the allocation model and report that activity to 
the Board at the next ensuing meeting. An ongoing exception is 
made for alternative asset classes, which may differ from the target 
ranges outlined for periods of time, due to the illiquid nature of the 
asset classes. In the event the existing allocation is within the
maximum/minimum guidelines (see V. D. below) no action may be 
taken.
The Board will review the overall fund allocation of assets at their 
annual review meeting. Significantly over-weighted asset classes may 
be cut back at that time, particularly those which fall outside the 
guideline allocations. Otherwise, the Board will rely on the advice of 
the Investment Consultant for changes to weightings or to the Asset 
Allocation model.
4. Acceptable Investment Risk:
The aggregate risk level appropriate for the retirement system is 
specified in this investment policy statement, which reflects the Fund’s 
characteristics, and liquidity requirements, keeping in mind the 
fiduciary purpose for which the assets are accumulated. The 
acceptable risk level is specified in Section V. D.
5. Asset Allocation Studies:
Periodic asset allocation studies may be considered annually by the 
Board which will:
a. Develop a long range rationale to guide the deployment of 
contributions and assets;
b. Identify appropriate expected risk/return parameters for the 
investment of System assets; and
c. Reassess the current investment policy as it pertains to the 
relationship between the System’s assets and liabilities.
6. Capital Market Assumptions:
Capital market assumptions are reviewed annually by the Board and the 
Investment Consultant. 
D. Asset Allocation Program
After careful consideration of the above referenced asset allocation 
factors, the Board has established a long-term asset allocation program 
that leads to an appropriate asset mix, realistic investment objectives and 
relevant investment constraints, as summarized on the next page:
